subject: chemistry
title: Stoichiometric Relationships Adventure 3: Yield, atom economy and limiting reagent
welcome_lead: Today you'll find the limiting reagent and calculate yields like an industrial chemist.
meta_desc: Chemistry — limiting reagent, percentage yield, atom economy, green chemistry.
final_note: You learned the limiting reagent caps the product, % yield = actual/theoretical × 100, and atom economy rewards efficient reactions.

walkthroughs.body_html:
For aA + bB → products:

1. Calculate moles of each reactant.
2. Divide each by its stoichiometric coefficient.
3. Smallest ratio = limiting reagent.

Example: 2 mol H₂ + 1 mol O₂ → H₂O.
n(H₂)/2 = 1.0; n(O₂)/1 = 1.0 → exactly balanced, no limiting.

% yield = (actual mass / theoretical mass) × 100

Lab makes 14.0 g aspirin from 18.0 g salicylic acid.
Theoretical: 18.0/138 × 180 = 23.5 g.
% yield = 14.0/23.5 × 100 = 59.6%.

Yield is always < 100% (side reactions, losses, equilibrium).

Atom economy = Mr(desired product) / Σ Mr(reactants) × 100

Substitution reactions have low atom economy (byproducts); addition reactions can be 100%.

Green chemistry (Anastas + Warner, 1998): 12 principles include high atom economy, renewable feedstocks, safer solvents — driving the chemical industry globally.

mcqs.q: If 25 g of product is obtained when 40 g is theoretical, % yield is:
What is reduction in terms of electrons?
options: Gain of electrons (the oxidation number is reduced).
Mass is spread evenly throughout the entire atom including the electron shells.
Reduction means losing oxygen and oxidation means gaining oxygen — full stop.
Reduction means a substance becomes physically smaller in size.

mcqs.q: Where is almost all the mass of an atom located?
options: Mass is spread evenly throughout the entire atom including the electron shells.
In the nucleus, made up of protons and neutrons.
The standard hydrogen electrode has a potential of -1 V to balance copper at +1 V.
Electrons contribute significantly to the mass of an atom.

mcqs.q: In a standard hydrogen electrode used as a reference, what is the assigned electrode potential?
options: The standard hydrogen electrode actually has zero potential because hydrogen has no charge.
The standard hydrogen electrode has a potential of -1 V to balance copper at +1 V.
Reduction means a substance becomes physically smaller in size.
Exactly 0 V by convention — all other electrode potentials are measured relative to it.
